### 1. Core Purpose & Value Proposition  
BEAST positions itself as a **governance layer** that sits between a coding agent (LLM‑based or otherwise) and the local development environment. Its primary claims are:

| Claim | What it means | Why it matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Bounded view of the repo** | The model only sees a small, relevant slice of the codebase rather than the whole repository. | Reduces token waste, hallucination, and the temptation to make sweeping, unnecessary changes. |
| **Bounded actions** | The model must return a narrowly‑scoped, schema‑validated action (e.g., “edit lines 12‑15 of file X”) instead of free‑form file rewrites. | Guarantees that the agent cannot unintentionally corrupt large sections of code. |
| **Local compilation & verification** | Proposed edits are applied locally, compiled (or lint‑checked), and the result is verified before being committed. | Catches syntax errors, type mismatches, or broken tests early, preventing “plausible‑looking but broken” patches. |
| **Rollback & memory** | Failed or unsafe actions are rolled back, and the system records what actually worked. | Provides a safety net and creates a traceable audit trail for debugging or compliance. |
| **Provider‑agnostic routing** | Works with VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, MCP clients, OpenAI‑compatible agents, Ollama, or custom orchestration. | Makes BEAST a flexible middleware that can be adopted without locking into a single vendor. |

Overall, BEAST addresses a well‑known failure mode of LLMs in software engineering: **over‑reach** (reading too much, editing too broadly, and ignoring local constraints). By enforcing a strict contract—*model proposes, BEAST resolves*—the system shifts the burden of correctness from the model to a deterministic, local verifier.

BEAST positions itself as a **governance layer** that sits between a coding agent (LLM‑based or otherwise) and the local development environment. Its primary claims are:

| Claim | What it means | Why it matters |

| **Provider‑agnostic routing** | Works with VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, MCP clients, OpenAI‑compatible agents, Ollama, or custom orchestration. | Makes BEAST a flexible middleware that can be adopted without locking into a single vendor. |

BEAST positions itself as a **governance layer** that sits between a coding agent (LLM‑based or otherwise) and the local development environment. Its primary claims are:

| Claim | What it means | Why it matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Bounded view of the repo** | The model only sees a small, relevant slice of the codebase rather than the whole repository. | Reduces token waste, hallucination, and the temptation to make sweeping, unnecessary changes. |
| **Bounded actions** | The model must return a narrowly‑scoped, schema‑validated action (e.g., “edit lines 12‑15 of file X”) instead of free‑form file rewrites. | Guarantees that the agent cannot unintentionally corrupt large sections of code. |
| **Local compilation & verification** | Proposed edits are applied locally, compiled (or lint‑checked), and the result is verified before being committed. | Catches syntax errors, type mismatches, or broken tests early, preventing “plausible‑looking but broken” patches. |
| **Rollback & memory** | Failed or unsafe actions are rolled back, and the system records what actually worked. | Provides a safety net and creates a traceable audit trail for debugging or compliance. |
| **Provider‑agnostic routing** | Works with VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, MCP clients, OpenAI‑compatible agents, Ollama, or custom orchestration. | Makes BEAST a flexible middleware that can be adopted without locking into a single vendor. |

Overall, BEAST addresses a well‑known failure mode of LLMs in software engineering: **over‑reach** (reading too much, editing too broadly, and ignoring local constraints). ### 1. Core Purpose & Value Proposition  
BEAST positions itself as a **governance layer** that sits between a coding agent (LLM‑based or otherwise) and the local development environment. Its primary claims are:

| Claim | What it means | Why it matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Bounded view of the repo** | The model only sees a small, relevant slice of the codebase rather than the whole repository. | Reduces token waste, hallucination, and the temptation to make sweeping, unnecessary changes. |
| **Bounded actions** | The model must return a narrowly‑scoped, schema‑validated action (e.g., “edit lines 12‑15 of file X”) instead of free‑form file rewrites. | Guarantees that the agent cannot unintentionally corrupt large sections of code. |
| **Local compilation & verification** | Proposed edits are applied locally, compiled (or lint‑checked), and the result is verified before being committed. | Catches syntax errors, type mismatches, or broken tests early, preventing “plausible‑looking but broken” patches. |
| **Rollback & memory** | Failed or unsafe actions are rolled back, and the system records what actually worked. | Provides a safety net and creates a traceable audit trail for debugging or compliance. |
| **Provider‑agnostic routing** | Works with VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, MCP clients, OpenAI‑compatible agents, Ollama, or custom orchestration. | Makes BEAST a flexible middleware that can be adopted without locking into a single vendor. |

Overall, BEAST addresses a well‑known failure mode of LLMs in software engineering: **over‑reach** (reading too much, editing too broadly, and ignoring local constraints). By enforcing a strict contract—*model proposes, BEAST resolves*—the system shifts the burden of correctness from the model to a deterministic, local verifier.

| BEAST‑rescued verified fixes | 11/24 | ~46% required local verification to turn a proposed patch into a correct one. |
| JSON validity / Schema validity | 100%/100% | The interface contract is reliably enforced. |
| Patch application | 100% | Every validated action could be applied without merge conflicts or file‑system errors. |

### 1. Core Purpose & Value Proposition 
BEAST positions itself as a **governance layer** that sits between a coding agent (LLM‑based or otherwise) and the local development environment. Its primary claims are:

| Claim | What it means | Why it matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Bounded view of the repo** | The model only sees a small, relevant slice of the codebase rather than the whole repository. | Reduces token waste, hallucination, and the temptation to make sweeping, unnecessary changes. |
| **Bounded actions** | The model must return a narrowly‑scoped, schema‑validated action (e.g., “edit lines 12‑15 of file X”) instead of free‑form file rewrites. | Guarantees that the agent cannot unintentionally corrupt large sections of code. |
| **Local compilation & verification** | Proposed edits are applied locally, compiled (or lint‑checked), and the result is verified before being committed. | Catches syntax errors, type mismatches, or broken tests early, preventing “plausible‑looking but broken” patches. |
| **Rollback & memory** | Failed or unsafe actions are rolled back, and the system records what actually worked. | Provides a safety net and creates a traceable audit trail for debugging or compliance. |
| **Provider‑agnostic routing** | Works with VS Code, Cursor, Claude Code, MCP clients, OpenAI‑compatible agents, Ollama, or custom orchestration. | Makes BEAST a flexible middleware that can be adopted without locking into a single vendor. |

Overall, BEAST addresses a well‑known failure mode of LLMs in software engineering: **over‑reach** (reading too much, editing too broadly, and ignoring local constraints). By enforcing a strict contract—*model proposes, BEAST resolves*—the system shifts the burden of correctness from the model to a deterministic, local verifier.

---

### 2. Evidence of Effectiveness 

#### a. xAI Omni‑Gauntlet (24 live governed tasks) 
| Metric | Result | Interpretation |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| Full‑BEAST verified completion | 24/24 | **100%** end‑to‑end success when BEAST is fully engaged. |
| Provider‑clean hidden‑passing fixes | 13/24 | ~54% of tasks were solved by the model *without* needing BEAST’s rescue—shows the model can sometimes succeed on its own. |
| BEAST‑rescued verified fixes | 11/24 | ~46% required local verification to turn a proposed patch into a correct one. |
| JSON validity / Schema validity | 100%/100% | The interface contract is reliably enforced. |
| Patch application | 100% | Every validated action could be applied without merge conflicts or file‑system errors. |
| Out‑of‑scope edits | 0% | No unintended modifications outside the allowed region. |
| Architecture layers covered | 13/13 | The system exercised a broad range of code‑base layers (e.g., UI, backend, config, tests). |
| Matched raw Grok completion | 1/4 | Baseline model performance (without BEAST) was low (25%); BEAST lifted verified completion to 100%. |

**Takeaway:** BEAST turned a **25%** baseline success rate into **100%** on this benchmark, with nearly half of the wins coming from the verifier’s ability to correct model proposals. This demonstrates a **significant safety and correctness lift**.
